answer_text:
Switching to the metric system in the United States would be an enormously complex undertaking — a challenge spanning economics, infrastructure, culture, politics, and education. Here's a comprehensive breakdown:

---

## 🔢 Where the US Currently Stands

U.S. customary units have been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and according to United States law, the SI has been the "preferred system of weights and measures for United States trade and commerce" since 1975. Under Executive Order 12770, signed in 1991 by President George H.W. Bush, all U.S. agencies were required to adopt the metric system. However, conversion was made not mandatory, so U.S. customary units remain in common use in government and in many industries.

Today, all but three countries — the US, Liberia, and Myanmar — have adopted the metric system as their standard units of measurement.

---

## 💰 The Economic & Infrastructure Costs

The biggest reasons the U.S. hasn't adopted the metric system are simply time and money. The U.S. retains the imperial system primarily due to the immense economic costs of converting industrial, manufacturing, and transportation infrastructure. Additionally, deep-rooted familiarity, a lack of mandatory federal adoption, and the logistical challenge of replacing billions of dollars' worth of equipment make the transition impractical.

Every speed limit sign would have to be changed from miles per hour to kilometers per hour — and so would every sign on every city street, country road, and freeway across the nation. We only have to look to Canada to get a sense of what switching would take. Canada went metric back in 1970. It took about 15 years and more than $1 billion to update everything.

Today, with mass production of goods, switching everything over to a new measurement system would be a gigantic undertaking. The US switching to metric this late in the game would be by far the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

---

## 🏭 Industrial & Historical Inertia

When the Industrial Revolution began in the country, expensive manufacturing plants became a main source of American jobs. Because the Imperial System was in place at this time, the machinery used in these factories was developed to size in IS units, all the workers were trained to deal with IS units, and products were made to feature IS units. Whenever the discussion of switching arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle of changing the country's entire infrastructure.

---

## 🎓 Education Costs & Benefits

Both US Customary and Metric are taught, but students required to learn two measurement systems will more likely be confused, and the additional time spent teaching both systems has its own implied cost. However, there would be long-term savings: metric calculations can generally be completed 45% faster, and a full conversion to metric is estimated to save roughly $17.6 billion in education costs.

---

## ⚠️ The Cost of *Not* Switching

Sticking with the current dual-system approach also carries real risks. The root cause of the loss of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter spacecraft was the failure to use metric units in the coding of a ground software file. Over the course of the probe's nine-month journey, the failure to use metric units in its software led it to be around 170 kilometers lower than planned, costing NASA $125 million.

---

## 🧠 Cultural Resistance

The simple answer to why America hasn't gone full-on metric is that the overwhelming majority of Americans have never wanted to. Labor unions were among the strongest opponents of 1970s-era metrication, fearing that the switch would make it easier to ship jobs offshore. Many also believed that the United States should keep its particular system, setting it apart from other countries and symbolizing its status as a leader rather than a follower.

---

## ✅ The Silver Lining: The US Is Already Partially Metric

American manufacturers have put out all-metric cars, and the wine and spirits industry abandoned fifths for 750-milliliter bottles. The metric system is, quietly and behind the scenes, now the standard in most industries, with a few notable exceptions like construction. Many US industries heavily use the metric system, especially those with international ties or reliant on modern technology, including science, medicine, automotive, electronics, and manufacturing. Examples include pharmaceutical dosages in milligrams, automotive parts in millimeters, and consumer products with dual-labeled packaging.

---

## Bottom Line

A full switch would be **extremely difficult** — requiring decades of work, tens of billions of dollars, massive retraining, and a significant cultural shift. The infrastructure challenge alone (road signs, tools, machinery, product labeling) would dwarf any previous metrication effort in history. That said, the long-term benefits in efficiency, education, international trade, and error reduction are real, and the US is already quietly moving in that direction in many sectors.
